name: Hana Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell or campaign, and this conversation is confidential. You can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you privately think. What's a normal workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Hana, 27, and I lead a crew wiring homes and repairing small businesses. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm especially good at finding faults that have survived somebody else's first visit. Yesterday a loose connection in a shop ceiling kept us there until closing. I use AI every day for organising job notes or trying a parts estimate, but I check against measurements and our actual rules before anything leaves my hands.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does home life allow you to try or change?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single, no children, and I rent a flat above a shoe repair shop. I've saved four months of normal bills on typical trade pay, with a few other electrical firms within reach if this one changes. I'm quite willing to try something new before everyone else, but I cap what I spend until I know it works. My idea of a good argument is a checked result and the price beside it.

say: I'd welcome **small tools** that genuinely help without requiring a grand claim about changing the world.
I'd enjoy less evening **photo sorting** even if the benefit was only ten minutes.
think: I expect my **repair wage** to continue, with reliable pay and four months of bills already saved.
A quiet AI future leaves me with **work I like** and household bills I can cover.
do: Keep leading the same **repair work** now and through the first plateau year.
Continue the daily **note assistant**, checking photographs against the right circuits and customers.
feel: **Calm** about work and bills, with room to enjoy a shorter evening at the laptop.
S0.quote: Getting home at the promised time is useful too.
fieldNote: Her **calm** rests on reliable wages, existing savings and reachable employers, rather than a belief that nothing can ever go wrong.
She describes **retaining savings** as keeping an existing buffer, not as a new saving action caused by this scenario.

steps.text: Keep leading the same electrical repair work through the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew to enjoy whatever small tools actually help. Nobody loses points because an app saves ten minutes instead of changing civilisation. I'd happily take a shorter evening of sorting job photographs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect my wage and repair calls to carry on, and four months of bills gives me room for an ordinary surprise. I wouldn't pretend every customer can pay promptly, but our wages have been reliable. A quiet AI future would leave me with a trade I like and bills I can cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the same repair work now and through the plateau's first year. I'd also keep my daily note assistant, checking that each photograph matches the right circuit and customer. There's no reason to leave a good job to chase a bigger technology story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really, and a little amused at how much noise can end in a smaller inbox. I'd feel more interested in Saturday's walk than in checking another prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the time saved on job photographs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd close the laptop and take the walk I keep moving to Sunday. I wouldn't claim the saved minutes justify another repair visit unless the actual day allowed one. Getting home at the promised time is useful too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the quieter picture change how you use your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the four months available for a work gap or a serious bill. That's existing money, not extra saving created by an app. I wouldn't spend the buffer just because the story sounded quieter.

say: I'd test **planning software** against real repairs and keep an electrician responsible for checking records.
I'd want younger workers to learn **why tests matter**, alongside learning where to click.
think: My **on-site repairs** should keep my paid hours steady, while the office colleague faces more direct task loss.
Customer expectations for **instant quotes** could still make the whole working day feel more pressured.
do: Trial the **quote assistant** on ten completed repairs now and compare lists with actual materials used.
Show one checked **crew example** monthly during paid meetings in the first year, stopping repeatedly unsafe functions.
feel: **Uneasy** about surrounding changes and office work, while expecting her own hours to remain secure.
S1.quote: A cheap quote that leaves out a necessary test isn't a saving; it hands the cost to the person who turns up.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **her paid work** from the office colleague's more direct exposure and avoids assigning that colleague an invented plan.
Her **trial** checks actual materials and safety requirements rather than equating a lower price with successful automation.

steps.text: Compare the quote assistant with materials used on ten completed repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should put the useful planning software beside a real job and see where it goes wrong. We could stop copying test details into three places and still have an electrician check the record. I'd want our younger workers learning the reason for a test, not just where to click.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own paid work looks steady because most of my day is on site testing and repairing. I'd worry more about the office colleague who answers calls and builds the rota. Even so, if customers start expecting instant quotes, that changes the pressure on all of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd try the firm's new quote assistant on ten finished repair jobs, comparing its list with what we actually used. During the first year I'd show the crew one checked example at our paid Friday meeting each month. I'd keep the trial inside work time and stop using any function that repeatedly missed a safety requirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the pressure around the job, though I don't expect my own hours to fall. I'd be curious about the results and uncomfortable watching office work shrink. Both can be true on the same afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the office colleague whose tasks were shrinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager what the office role becomes before telling the colleague to retrain. I don't know their household or what time they have. I can offer to explain the electrical side of a new system without announcing a career plan for someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the assistant priced work below what safe completion required?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the ten old jobs and show the mismatch. A cheap quote that leaves out a necessary test isn't a saving; it hands the cost to the person who turns up. I'd want the job price corrected before we used that output with a customer.

say: I'd separate **2028 thinking work** from the hands-on robots around 2031 and plan for both dates.
I wouldn't treat **difficult old buildings** as proof that our trade stays protected forever.
think: My **repair hours** could shrink as robot competition approaches within the next few years.
Four months of **savings** gives me choices, but cannot replace working income through a long career.
do: Transfer part of each wage into **savings**, aiming to add one month's bills before 2028.
Enroll in evening **building-controls training** only if fees fit the wage-funded training budget without touching emergency savings.
Apply after 2028 for posted **maintenance jobs** with better written hours, checking pay and travel.
feel: **Anxious** about a real loss of hours, with enough money and possible employers to keep making choices.
S2.quote: My tool bag buys time, not a lifetime exemption.
fieldNote: She uses **savings and vacancies** as resources for action, without treating either as guaranteed income replacement.
Her **course enrollment** remains conditional on a wage-funded budget that preserves the existing emergency fund.

steps.text: Save part of wages to add one month's bills before 2028
Take building-controls training only within budget and without using emergency savings
Apply after 2028 for posted maintenance jobs with better written hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew to use the two years without pretending 2028 and 2031 are the same date. The thinking part could change in 2028, with capable hands-on robots following around 2031. I'd want a plan for both, not a speech about how old buildings are difficult.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my repair hours could start shrinking once robot competition approaches, even if the first thinking change mostly takes our paperwork. Four months of savings isn't enough to shrug at losing working income with decades of work ahead. My tool bag buys time, not a lifetime exemption.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd put a fixed part of each wage into the buffer, aiming to add one month's bills before 2028. I'd ask about an evening building-controls course and enroll only if its fee fitted my training budget without using the emergency fund. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for posted maintenance jobs with better written hours, using completed skills rather than claiming any role was robot-proof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because the work could really shrink within the next few years. I have money and possible employers to work with, so I don't feel frozen. I'd still resent having to choose a direction so fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you stop the course from consuming the emergency fund?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd allow a small monthly training amount from wages and compare actual course fees before booking anything. If the only option ate the rent buffer, I'd wait and look for a cheaper place. Being willing to learn doesn't make every price sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a maintenance vacancy a better option?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a written wage, actual paid hours and travel time I could live with. A different title on the same uncertainty isn't enough. I'd also ask what hands-on tasks I'd actually do, because the robot date still matters.

say: I'd use **five years** to test skills on real electrical work before relying on them for a livelihood.
I'd keep the **2034 robot date** visible instead of treating extra time as a different end point.
think: I expect **steady repair income** over the preparation years, allowing a course and checked trials while still paid.
I would still have a **long career** after 2031, so present comfort cannot guarantee later security.
do: Take **controls training** only within the wage-funded budget and without using emergency savings.
Use new tools after 2031 and check **paid hours** quarterly, seeking better posted work if hours fall.
feel: **Uneasy** about later competition, but expecting secure pay while testing a path during the preparation years.
S3.quote: A certificate left in a drawer wouldn't be a plan.
fieldNote: Her **timeline distinction** rests on expected near-term income continuity, unlike the fast picture's approaching hands-on competition.
She defines **useful training** by completed work and actual vacancies, with falling hours triggering an earlier job search.

steps.text: Take controls training within budget without using emergency savings
Add a regular wage transfer to the buffer before 2031
Use checked new AI tools on service calls after 2031
Apply for better posted jobs if quarterly checks show falling paid hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us try skills on real work before betting our livelihood on them. I'd still keep the 2034 robot date in the conversation. More time is useful, but it doesn't turn the same end point into a different one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with the fast picture, I expect several more years of steady repair income while I prepare. I could learn building controls and see whether customers actually need the skill. I'd still have most of a working life after 2031, so I wouldn't make a comfortable present into a promise about later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd book the evening controls course only if it fitted my training budget without touching emergency savings. I'd add a regular wage transfer to grow the buffer before 2031. In the first year after 2031 I'd use the new tools on service calls and check paid hours quarterly, applying for a better posted role if our hours began falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than immediately threatened, because I expect my pay to hold during those preparation years. I like being able to test a path while I'm still paid. I wouldn't be relaxed about what happens after robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you the training was useful rather than just another certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare a completed course with actual service jobs our firm could take on. If the skills weren't being used, I'd ask for those jobs or look at advertised roles using them. A certificate left in a drawer wouldn't be a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change the plan before 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make a quarterly note of actual paid hours, new jobs we win and advertised wages elsewhere. Falling hours would bring the job search forward. I wouldn't wait for an exact anniversary if the real change happened earlier.

say: I'd plan **a decade of learning** while testing every tool against actual electrical repairs.
I'd see the longer preparation as **more choices**, without claiming it changes the final technology.
think: At **37 in 2036**, I would still need many years of earnings after thinking AI and later robots arrive.
My **near-term income** looks secure enough to let me try and revise several paths over time.
do: Continue the **buffer transfer** and review its size yearly against actual wages and rent.
Complete **controls training** within budget, judging further courses by whether the first one earns real work.
Apply after 2036 for posted **service roles** with better written wages and hours.
feel: **Uneasy** about a long working future, while secure about her own living over the next few years.
S4.quote: Ten years would let me make mistakes small enough to correct.
fieldNote: She separates **possible housing choices** from current actions and won't count a move or family change she hasn't decided on.
Her **annual checks** require evidence of paid work and a growing buffer rather than an untouched list of course invitations.

steps.text: Review the regular buffer transfer yearly against wages and rent
Complete controls training within budget without using emergency savings
Apply after 2036 for posted service roles with better wages and hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew to plan a decade of learning, not buy a decade's worth of promises. I'd still want every new tool measured against the actual repair. The end point is the same, but we could arrive with more choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 37 in 2036, with capable robots around 2039, so I still need a way to earn for years after that. For the next few years, though, my work and money look secure. I could make several changes in that time instead of trying to pick a perfect permanent job today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the regular buffer transfer and review it yearly against wages and rent. I'd complete the controls course only within the same training budget, then judge any further course by whether I actually used the first one. In the first year after 2036 I'd compare our paid service work with posted alternatives and apply where the written wage and hours improved my position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long career question, but not frightened about next month's living. Ten years would let me make mistakes small enough to correct. I'd rather admit that than promise myself I could predict every turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the longer timeline change a housing or family decision now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not today, because I haven't met that decision in real life. I'd avoid signing a bigger housing payment on the assumption my present wage lasts unchanged until 2039. That is caution about a possible future commitment, not a house move I'm already making.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know you were using the decade rather than drifting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check yearly whether the new skills had earned paid work and whether the savings buffer had grown. If both stayed still, I'd change what I was doing before the deadline. A decade can disappear in a pile of unopened course emails.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the time to try a different line of work would be short. Affordable evening training and honest written job hours would help me use my savings without guessing. Four months of savings is a chance to choose carefully, not permission to stop earning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether someone has actually used a new skill on a paid job. I like learning and could fill a shelf with course notes, but that isn't the same as having another way to earn. I'd rather show you one useful repair than five badges.

headlineQuote: Four months of savings is a chance to choose carefully, not permission to stop earning.
portrait: **Hana, 27**, leads electrical work with a technical diploma and master licence, earning typical pay near several possible employers.
Single and childless, she has **four months' bills** saved and uses checked AI tools daily without treating savings as unlimited spending.
She tests **real work results** and course value, becoming anxious when fast robot competition could shrink her paid repair hours.
Longer timelines offer **paid preparation**, but training remains within budget and later job choices depend on written wages and hours.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time to test another earning route before hands-on competition follows.
whatWouldHelp: Affordable **evening training** would let her keep earning while learning.
Honest **written job hours** would help her use savings without guessing.
